text: French students are now showing the world how we should be standing up and how we should be revolting against an extremely violent system. They've been going for almost three weeks now, students occupying the school, people are stepping up and revolting and rebelling against the system. We know it's not working in our favor, which we can also see from the extremely violent response from the establishment. So what is actually happening in France? Are these really high school students protesting against poor conditions in their school? Or are we witnessing riots by Arab and African Islamists, as some people claim? Because depending on whom you listen to, you might get completely different explanations of what's happening. For example, on October 6th, U.S. President Donald Trump wrote on True Social, what is happening in France is nothing else than out-of-control mass migration. He continued, this isn't about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great country. But Jean-Luc Melenchon, the leader of the French left-wing party La France Insoumise, has a rather different interpretation. On September 28th, he wrote on X that protesting high school students were harmless, accused the government of ordering a crackdown with racist undertones, and called on members of his party to intervene between the students and the police. Meanwhile, Marine Le Pen, one of France's most prominent right-wing politicians, argued that these were no longer student protests, but organized riots involving professional troublemakers, allegedly supported by members of Melenchon's party. She also called for a new law against rioters. And French President Emmanuel Macron acknowledged the concerns of young people while condemning the violence and accusing certain politicians of encouraging the unrest. So interestingly, even Le Pen wasn't making quite the same argument as Trump. While Trump blamed Islam and immigration, Le Pen focused on organized violence and the involvement of the radical left. So who is right? Are these genuine student protests? Are Islamists responsible for the violence? Is the radical left involved? Or could several different things be happening at the same time? And these explanations are not necessarily mutually exclusive. A protest movement can have legitimate demands while some of its participants commit crimes. And other people can use an existing protest as an opportunity for violence, even if they have little interest in its original goals. So I want to look at what actually happened, how the protests developed, and what we know about the people involved. And I think it makes sense to start with how it all began. In mid-September, teachers at Saint-Exupéry High School in Créteil, a suburb of Paris, protested against staff shortages and insufficient resources at their school. Their students soon joined them, blocking the school entrance to demand better conditions. And when I say students, I'm not primarily talking about university students. These were high school students, typically between 15 and 18 years old. In France, these schools are called lycées and their students are known as lycéens. Their demands were fairly straightforward. They wanted more teachers, better school buildings, less overcrowded classrooms, and improvements to their schedules. Some also demanded changes to parcours soup, the system used for university admissions, which they argued disadvantaged students from less privileged schools. And these complaints were not entirely unfounded. According to the French Ministry of Education, in the 2024-2025 school year, students in public secondary schools missed 15.4 million hours of lessons because absent teachers were not replaced. That represented 7.5% of scheduled teaching hours. So there were real problems in the education system. Whether all the students' demands were reasonable and whether the government could afford to meet them is a separate question. But what started as a local school protest quickly spread. Videos circulated on social media, students at other schools organized similar actions, and high school student unions began coordinating demonstrations. By September 28th, around 180 schools across France were affected. Just three days later, on October 1st, that number had grown to more than 1,000 schools, including over 200 where entrances were blockaded. And the movement was no longer limited to high school students. University students began joining, along with teachers, parents, trade unions, and other groups. By October 6th, the French Interior Ministry estimated that approximately 266,000 people had participated in demonstrations across the country. Organizers claimed the number was closer to 450,000. Either way, this was no longer a small local protest. But as the movement grew, so did the violence. Some schools were vandalized or set on fire. Protesters threw fireworks and other objects at police officers, damaged public property, and blocked roads. There were also reports of attacks on teachers and other school employees. And clashes with the police left people injured on both sides, including teenagers who suffered serious injuries during police operations. Importantly, violence was already occurring in the early stages of the movement. It wasn't as though everyone protested peacefully for several weeks and then suddenly decided to start rioting. But there is another important distinction here. The fact that violence happened during demonstrations doesn't mean everyone participating in those demonstrations was violent. And the situation became even more complicated as other groups joined the movement. By mid-October, the protests had expanded beyond education. People were also demonstrating against rising living costs, low wages, and problems with public services. Then, on October 17th, another major wave of demonstrations took place across France. This time, the movement brought together high school and university students, trade unions, yellow vest activists, and other groups dissatisfied with the government. The Interior Ministry estimated that around 550,000 people participated nationwide, while organizers claimed approximately 800,000. And once again, most demonstrations were peaceful, but some were accompanied by serious violence. In Paris, businesses were looted, vehicles were set on fire, and protesters clashed with police. Similar incidents occurred in other cities. In Limoges, rioters set fire to the historic town hall, causing extensive destruction, including the collapse of part of its roof and tower. So what began with teachers asking for better working conditions had, within a month, developed into a nationwide protest movement accompanied by serious riots. And I think there are two important things to recognize here. First, the original movement was real. It was started over genuine problems in the French education system, and it attracted large numbers of students and other supporters. Second, the violence was also real. And acknowledging the legitimacy of the original complaints doesn't somehow justify burning schools, attacking people, or destroying public property. But this still leaves us with the most controversial question. Who are the people actually committing the violence? Are they mostly high school students? Immigrants and their descendants? Radical left activists? Or as Donald Trump and some other commentators have suggested, Islamists? That is what I want to take a closer look at in the next part.
